mappings.note: Tests that even wholly biodegradable waste still burdens the environment - the biodegradable side of C 4.1-LO-1's consequences clause. DEFECT: near-duplicate of qid:87213 with a values rider added.

Burning plastic judged against segregated disposal is LO-3's 'evaluates methods of waste disposal'; deciding which leftovers go in which bin needs the biodegradable/non-biodegradable split of C 4.1-LO-1. Both halves are asked.
Composting versus two dustbins is a comparison of disposal methods (C 4.3-LO-3); the comparison only works if the student knows which wastes can be composted (C 4.1-LO-1).
Part (a) is decomposers acting on biodegradable matter (C 4.1-LO-1); part (b) is unidirectional energy flow (C 2.8-LO-1). The two parts sit under different competencies.
Pesticides reaching fruit juice and then accumulating in organs - biomagnification, which happens because the residues are non-biodegradable, C 4.1-LO-1.
Ozone formation with equation, its usefulness and the substances that deplete it - all three parts fall inside C 4.3-LO-2's causes, effects and measures clauses.
Parts (a) and (b) are trophic levels and energy flow (C 2.8-LO-1); part (c) asks for an ecological pyramid, whose narrowing is the ten per cent law (C 2.8-LO-2).

Green plants as producers - the first trophic level of every food chain, C 2.8-LO-1.
Assertion-reason tying 'producer' to photosynthesis - why plants hold the first trophic level, C 2.8-LO-1.
Names the food chain from its definition - C 2.8-LO-1's head clause.
Builds a terrestrial and an aquatic chain with trophic levels marked - 'constructs food chains', C 2.8-LO-1. No energy quantities are asked, so LO-2 is not engaged.
Every chain starts with a producer - a structural rule of food chains, C 2.8-LO-1.
The ten per cent figure itself - C 2.8-LO-2.
States the ten per cent law and accounts for the missing ninety per cent - C 2.8-LO-2, the outcome that owns the law.
Assertion-reason linking short chains to the ten per cent law - C 2.8-LO-2 verbatim ('explain why food chains are limited in length').
10000 J at the producers gives 1000 J at the primary consumers - one application of the ten per cent law, C 2.8-LO-2.
Derives both short chains and the narrowing pyramid from the ten per cent law - C 2.8-LO-2 at its fullest.
Identifies the biodegradable option - LO-1's classification clause.
Corrects the claim that plastic is biodegradable - LO-1's distinction clause.
Four-way match sorting peel, glass, cotton and polythene by biodegradability - C 4.1-LO-1 across all four pairs.
Locating the frog's trophic level in a given chain - reading a food chain, C 2.8-LO-1, with no energy arithmetic.
Answer is explicitly the ten per cent law limiting chain length - C 2.8-LO-2. Stored concept tag 'Trophic Levels' points at LO-1, which would not explain the limit.
Herbivore as the plant-eating trophic role - vocabulary for constructing a food chain, C 2.8-LO-1.
Matches grass, goat, tiger and fungus to producer, herbivore, carnivore and decomposer - the roles used to build a food chain, C 2.8-LO-1. No energy quantity is involved, so LO-2 does not apply.
CFCs as the chief ozone-depleting chemicals - the causes clause of C 4.3-LO-2.
Formation, depletion and the international response - the causes, effects and measures clauses of C 4.3-LO-2 in one item.
Corrects the confusion between harmful ground-level ozone and the protective stratospheric layer - the function half of C 4.3-LO-2.
Decomposers break down dead organic matter and return nutrients; biodegradation is owned by C 4.1-LO-1. C 2.8-LO-1 concerns energy flow, and energy is not what decomposers return.
Assertion-reason on whether an ecosystem could work without decomposers - again the biodegradation clause of C 4.1-LO-1, this time with a false assertion.
Pesticide is highest at the top level because it is non-biodegradable and retained - C 4.1-LO-1. No chain is supplied to order, so the food-chain outcome is not indispensable.
Why humans, feeding at the top of several chains, carry the heaviest load - the consequences clause of C 4.1-LO-1.
Biomagnification defined, illustrated and its danger stated - all of it follows from the substance being non-biodegradable, C 4.1-LO-1.
Assertion-reason: a 'safe' concentration in water is not safe once retained and magnified - precisely the non-biodegradable consequence in C 4.1-LO-1.
Traces a non-biodegradable pesticide from spraying through soil, water and food chains - the fullest form of C 4.1-LO-1's consequences clause.

Computes a magnification factor of 12500 and interprets it - a quantitative biomagnification item, C 4.1-LO-1. It is not the ten per cent law, so C 2.8-LO-2 would be the wrong sibling despite the arithmetic.
Why energy flow is unidirectional - C 2.8-LO-1's 'flow of energy through trophic levels'. The item asks about direction, not the ten per cent figure.
Matter cycles but energy does not - the same directional property of energy flow, C 2.8-LO-1.
The stored answer derives the decline in numbers and biomass from the ten per cent law - C 2.8-LO-2, not the general flow statement of LO-1.
Corrects the claim that energy cycles - the unidirectional flow clause of C 2.8-LO-1.
20000 J at the grass leaves 200 J at the lion over two transfers - the ten per cent law applied twice, C 2.8-LO-2.
Why a web describes an ecosystem better than one chain - food webs are named only in C 2.8-LO-1.
Food chain versus food web and why the web is more realistic - C 2.8-LO-1's 'constructs food chains and food webs'.
Drawing the web with trophic levels is C 2.8-LO-1; the item additionally requires annotating the energy LOST at each step, which is the ten per cent law, C 2.8-LO-2.
Biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem - ecosystem structure, which no outcome in this frame covers, so competency C 4.3.
Components of an ecosystem and how they interact - competency C 4.3 ('interactions that take place at each level'); the producer/consumer/decomposer naming is incidental to the structural question.
Ecosystem defined, components named, natural distinguished from artificial - all ecosystem structure, competency C 4.3, with no LO reaching it.

Classifies consumers as herbivore, carnivore, omnivore and parasite - the competency C 4.1's own words, 'the ecological role organisms play (autotrophic or heterotrophic nutrition)'. Parasites are not a trophic level, so C 2.8-LO-1 would not be true of the whole item, and C 4.1-LO-1 is about biodegradability.
Why non-biodegradable substances are a problem - the consequences clause of C 4.1-LO-1.
Names biological magnification - the accumulation of a non-biodegradable toxin, C 4.1-LO-1.
Why the ozone layer matters to life - the effects half of C 4.3-LO-2, as against its causes half.
Evaluates the Montreal-style international response - LO-2's 'measures taken to limit it', taken to an assessment level.
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet - the protective function inside C 4.3-LO-2.
Labelled diagram annotating ozone formation and depletion - the causes clause of C 4.3-LO-2 in diagram form.
Reduce, reuse, recycle - LO-3's 'proposes ways of reducing the waste a household generates'.
Landfill, incineration and composting weighed against their drawbacks - LO-3's 'evaluates methods of waste disposal' exactly.
Completes the three Rs with 'recycle' - the waste-reduction clause of C 4.3-LO-3.
What an individual can realistically do about waste, starting from segregation at source - LO-3's proposal clause, judged rather than listed.
